While macOS is generally very stable, applications occasionally crash, and your Mac will ask whether you want to send a diagnostic report to Apple.

Researchers have discovered new Mac malware that mimics such dialog boxes and asks you to enter your Mac password as part of a data collection process. Once you do so, attackers can gain access to a large amount of personal data, including your password manager and cryptocurrency wallets...

According to Jamf, they began tracking this malware as early as May this year, and real-world attack cases have now been observed.

The cybersecurity firm pointed out that the disk image file used to spread the malware originally had a valid Apple Developer ID and was notarized, allowing it to pass Gatekeeper checks.

The point of entry is a disk image named "Werkbit Setup" with the mount path /Volumes/Werkbit Setup, containing an application bundle called Werkbit.app. Its executable is named veltod, and the bundle identifier is dev.golove.velto. Unlike the final malware payload itself, this dropper has proper code signing and notarization: it is a universal binary (supporting both arm64 and x86_64), signed with Developer ID Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV), has hardened runtime enabled, and comes with a stapled notarization ticket. Notably, the disk image itself is also signed, not just the application inside it, which is

Macworld reports that Apple has revoked the relevant certificate, so Gatekeeper should now be able to detect it. However, everyone should remain vigilant. In addition to watching out for the disk image mentioned above, you should also carefully examine any application crash reports and any password prompts claiming that "System Preferences" is requesting changes.

As always, the best protection is to download apps only from the Mac App Store and from the websites of developers you trust.
